prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, which brought atomic time-keeping to the 10^-18 level of accuracy and stability

statement.case_for: After reading all eight round-1 statements and the chair's questions, I keep the optical lattice clock as a single-part prize. The scientific content is a proposal and a realisation: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes the conflict between trapping many neutral atoms and perturbing the clock transition, and the strontium lattice clock, with Ye's work on record stability and systematic control, showed that the idea reaches the 10^-18 regime. That result has been reproduced and compared across independent national laboratories, the interpretation is not in dispute, and the instrument is already used for tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and searches for new physics. The two-name credit maps one-to-one onto the two steps, which is the cleanest attribution on the shortlist, and about two decades of confirmation make it mature. I treat the pending redefinition of the second as supporting context only. After Danielsson's and Lindroth's points I would not make the case depend on it, and the citation I propose does not mention it.
statement.case_against: Round 1 sharpened the objections rather than removing them. Novelty relative to the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize for quantum control of single ions is a real question, and Johansson, Mehlig and Olsson are right that I cannot dismiss it. Eriksson's point that this is an instrument-defining achievement and not a new regime of matter is a legitimate difference in what the committee values, and the fundamental-physics results the clocks should enable have not yet arrived. A two-name credit also leaves out other early lattice-clock groups and the ion clocks, and Olsson notes that nothing forces the committee to decide this year. Topological insulators have the broadest opening support and the longest independent confirmation, and the committee could fairly judge that a conceptual reorganisation of condensed matter outweighs a precision-measurement advance. I also recognise that I am the member closest to this field, which makes it more important that the case rests on the published record.

responses.point: Johansson asks whether Ye's frequency-comb overlap with the 2005 prize weakens the novelty of B034 relative to B028, and says B028 created a new class of quantum matter whereas B034 is greater precision in an established technique.
responses.response: On novelty, the 2005 prize recognised the comb as a tool for counting optical frequencies, and the 2012 prize recognised control of single trapped ions. The lattice clock is a different scheme. Its key idea is the magic wavelength, which lets thousands of neutral atoms be interrogated at once without light-shift errors, and that is Katori's proposal, not a comb result. Ye's credited contribution is the realisation and the many-body systematic control, not the comb itself. I therefore weigh the overlap as modest. I accept that the classification of topological matter is conceptually broader, and I keep B028 as my first alternative. But breadth of concept is not the only meaning of discovery or invention in the Nobel will, and a new method that changes what can be measured qualifies. Your point about attribution also stands: the trio you propose leaves out Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Fu, Moore and Balents, and I cannot weigh that against the clock's tidier credit as if it were a minor matter.

responses.point: Eriksson says B034 is more an instrument achievement than a new regime of matter, that several fundamental-physics results it should enable have not arrived, and that he would not block it, and he is open to recognising B028 before B046.
responses.response: I agree with part of this. The clock is an instrument, and I am not claiming it opened a new state of matter. The distinction I would draw is that its significance is already demonstrated by measurements that exist, not by promised ones. The relativistic redshift across millimetre-to-centimetre height differences, clock-to-clock comparisons at 10^-18 between different laboratories, and limits on drifts of constants are results in hand. I would not rest the case on the redefinition or on constraints that have not yet been obtained. Where I move toward you is on twisted bilayer graphene: your own maturity point (eight years, unsettled pairing mechanism, Cao outside the names) is the reason I keep B046 as a second alternative. Your willingness to support B028 first if B046 is deferred makes me think the committee's realistic choice is between B028 and B034, and I will say so in the vote.

responses.point: Mehlig says a clear credit list does not make a discovery more fundamental, that the clock's largest consequence has not happened, and that he would back B034 as the strongest precision-measurement option if the committee wants a mature and tidy case.
responses.response: I accept that clean attribution is not a measure of fundamental depth, and I have not argued that it is. It is a necessary condition for a prize that the committee can defend, and B034 meets it where the other leading candidates do not. On the point that the clock's main consequence has not occurred, I now treat the redefinition as context only. The case stands on what is demonstrated: the magic-wavelength lattice, accuracy at 10^-18 and the independent reproduction. I note that you identify B034 as your fallback, and that the mature-and-tidy criterion you state is the one I think the committee should apply, given that B046 has maturity problems you acknowledge and B028 has an allocation problem.

responses.point: Pearce proposes pairing B034 with a second part for IceCube credited to Halzen alone, and says the astroparticle part falls away if a single name cannot be justified; he also asks that my Hall-laboratory link be declared and handled openly.
responses.response: I do not support adding B005. A one-name credit for a detector built and analysed by a collaboration of hundreds, with the AMANDA precursor, the construction leaders and the analysis teams that found the 2013 flux uncredited, is not something I could defend to outside readers, and you yourself describe it as the weakest element. Combining it with the clock would also join two unconnected subjects, and a clean single-achievement prize is stronger than a two-part prize with one fragile half. On the disclosure, I agree it should be open and I restate it below. I would also not treat other lattice-clock groups as ruled out of consideration. I think the committee can defend the Katori-Ye pair as the proposal and the realisation that defined the scheme, while acknowledging in the deliberation that Lemonde, Ludlow, Lisdat, Bloom and others made important demonstrations.

responses.point: Lindroth supports B034 with the same two names, wants the case to rest on independent agreement of clocks and on the atomic-structure physics, and says my disclosure bears on whether I should take part in any final decision on this candidate.
responses.response: I agree that the case should stand independently of my view, and I have tried to cite only things that can be checked: independent national-laboratory comparisons at 10^-18, and the control of polarizability, multipole and blackbody shifts that you describe as essential to reaching that regime. That atomic-structure work is a good reason to regard the achievement as physics and not only engineering. On participation, I think my declared link is a perceived proximity, not a stake in the outcome, and I defer to the chair on whether it requires recusal. If the committee prefers, I can step back from the final decision on B034 specifically and leave the vote on that part to the other members.

responses.point: Danielsson says the redefinition of the second should not add to the merit, since the prize should rest on what was discovered or achieved and not on an administrative event, and he names B034 as the best fallback if B028's allocation is judged too contested.
responses.response: I agree and I have changed my position on this. In round 1 I cited the pending redefinition as supporting evidence of maturity. After your point I have taken it out of the citation and out of the core argument, since the merit is the accuracy, reproducibility and use of the clocks, not the metrological decision that may follow. I also note that you accept B034 as the fallback if Mele and Hasan cannot be resolved. If the committee keeps the topological-insulator trio of Kane, Mele and Molenkamp, I would accept that outcome as scientifically sound, and my remaining objection to it is only the unresolved attribution and the 2016 overlap.

uncertainties: How far the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 prize for single-ion control should lower the novelty of the lattice clock, which I judge modest but cannot settle from the record.
Whether a two-name credit can be defended against Lemonde, Ludlow, Lisdat, Bloom and other early lattice-clock groups, and how to treat ion clocks in the citation.
Whether the committee should treat the choice as mainly between B028 and B034, and whether the breadth and longer confirmation of topological insulators outweighs the cleaner credit of the clock.
Whether the committee is willing to recognise a measurement-method invention ahead of the redefinition of the second, which I regard as supporting context and not a precondition.
statement.conflict_note: Disclosure unchanged from round 1 and noted in the chair's summary. My doctoral period included a research stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder, and I am an atomic physicist at Lund who knows this field and some of its participants professionally. I report this as possible perceived proximity to the Hall and Ye environment, not a documented relationship with Katori or Ye and not a stake in the outcome. I have no documented connection to the candidates in B028, B046 or B005. I leave it to the chair whether recusal from the B034 vote is warranted, and I am willing to step back from that part if the committee wishes.
